lessons.title: The EM Spectrum and its Risks

before.content_html:
The Electromagnetic Spectrum

The electromagnetic (EM) spectrum is a continuous family of transverse waves. All EM waves share three essential properties: they transfer energy, they can travel through a vacuum (they do not need a medium), and they all travel at the same speed in a vacuum — the speed of light, which is \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Because speed is constant, waves with shorter wavelength have higher frequency, and vice versa.

The spectrum is arranged in order of increasing frequency (or decreasing wavelength). A useful mnemonic for the order is: Running Men In Vests Usually X-ray Giraffes — radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

Key Fact

All EM waves: travel at \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum, are transverse, carry energy, need no medium. Order (lowest to highest frequency): radio → microwave → infrared → visible → UV → X-ray → gamma.

Uses of Each EM Wave Type

Each region of the spectrum is suited to different applications because of its wavelength and energy. The properties that make a wave useful are the same properties that can make it dangerous if misused or overexposed.

Radio waves have the longest wavelengths and lowest frequencies. They are used for AM and FM radio broadcasting, television signals, and some forms of long-range communication. Long-wavelength radio waves can diffract over hills and buildings, enabling reception in shadowed areas. Radio waves are generally considered non-harmful at typical exposure levels. Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits, and can themselves induce oscillations in electrical circuits — this is how radio receivers work.

Microwaves are shorter than radio waves and are used in satellite communication, mobile phone networks, Wi-Fi, and microwave ovens. In ovens, microwaves cause water molecules in food to vibrate, producing internal heating. At the power levels used in communication devices, microwaves are considered non-ionising and low risk, though exposure to very intense microwave beams can heat body tissue.

Infrared radiation is emitted by all objects above absolute zero. It is used in remote controls, thermal imaging cameras, night-vision equipment, and optical fibre communications. Overexposure causes skin burns and can damage retinal tissue in the eye.

Visible light is the only part of the EM spectrum that human eyes can detect. It is used in photography, fibre optic cables, and vision itself. Lasers (a form of focused visible light) are used in surgery, engineering measurements, and barcode scanners. Very intense light (such as looking directly at a laser or the sun) can damage the retina.

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation causes skin tanning, sunburn, and — with repeated overexposure — increases the risk of skin cancer by damaging DNA in skin cells. UV is used in fluorescent lamps, detecting forged banknotes (security ink fluoresces under UV), and sterilising medical equipment. The ozone layer in the atmosphere absorbs much of the UV from the Sun.

X-rays penetrate soft tissue but are absorbed by bone and metal. This makes them invaluable in medical imaging — an X-ray photograph shows bones and dense structures clearly. They are also used in airport security scanners to examine luggage. X-rays are ionising radiation: they can remove electrons from atoms, damaging DNA and potentially causing mutations or cancer. Medical staff and security workers take precautions (lead shielding, limiting exposure time) to keep doses to a minimum. This principle is known as ALARA — As Low As Reasonably Achievable.

Gamma rays have the highest frequency and the greatest energy of all EM waves. They are emitted by radioactive nuclei. Because they are highly penetrating and ionising, they are used to treat cancer (radiotherapy targets tumours) and to sterilise medical instruments. They can also cause serious cell damage and cancer if exposure is uncontrolled. Strict safety protocols govern all medical and industrial use of gamma sources.

Ionising vs Non-Ionising Radiation

A critical distinction in radiation safety is between ionising radiation and non-ionising radiation. Ionising radiation (UV, X-rays, gamma rays) has sufficient energy to knock electrons out of atoms, creating charged ions. These ions can damage DNA, potentially leading to cell mutations and cancer. Non-ionising radiation (radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light) does not ionise atoms, so is generally lower risk, though intense beams of any type can still cause harm through heating.

Key Fact

Ionising (can damage DNA): UV, X-rays, gamma rays. Non-ionising (lower risk): radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light. Danger generally increases with frequency because higher-frequency waves carry more energy per photon.

Risk, Benefit and the ALARA Principle

Every medical use of ionising radiation involves a risk-benefit decision. The risk of DNA damage from a single chest X-ray is very small — far less than the risk of missing an undiagnosed lung condition. A radiotherapy dose is high enough to damage cancer cells, but is aimed carefully to minimise harm to healthy tissue. The ALARA principle guides all decisions about radiation exposure in medical, industrial, and research settings. This is a live example of how science informs decisions under uncertainty — evidence about risk at low doses is still being gathered and debated.

practice_questions.text: State two properties shared by all electromagnetic waves.
practice_questions.marks: Any two of: all travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum; all are transverse waves; all transfer energy; all can travel through a vacuum (do not need a medium) — 1 mark each. Mastering: two distinct properties correctly stated. Secure: two properties. Developing: one correct property. Emerging: vague or incorrect statement.

practice_questions.text: A patient needs a chest X-ray. Explain one benefit and one risk of using X-rays for this medical purpose, and describe how the risk is managed using the ALARA principle.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: benefit — X-rays penetrate soft tissue but are absorbed by bone and dense structures, enabling diagnosis of fractures, infections, or tumours (2); risk — X-rays are ionising radiation that can damage DNA and potentially cause cancer (2); ALARA — the dose is kept to the minimum needed for a clear image; staff use lead shielding and limit frequency of exposure; benefit of diagnosis outweighs small risk of a single X-ray (2). Secure: 4–5 marks. Developing: 2–3 marks. Emerging: 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain why gamma rays are more dangerous than radio waves, referring to ionisation in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: gamma rays have a much higher frequency (and shorter wavelength) than radio waves (1); higher frequency means more energy per wave — enough to remove electrons from atoms (ionise them) (1); ionisation can damage DNA in cells, potentially causing mutations or cancer; radio waves do not have enough energy to ionise and are considered non-ionising (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: one point.

practice_questions.text: Describe how ultraviolet radiation is both useful and potentially harmful. Refer to scientific evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: UV is useful — it causes fluorescence used in security marking and detecting forged banknotes; used in fluorescent lamps; triggers vitamin D production in skin (1+1); UV is harmful — overexposure causes sunburn; repeated overexposure damages DNA in skin cells, increasing risk of skin cancer (1); the evidence linking UV exposure to increased skin cancer rates is well-established from epidemiological studies (1); this illustrates that the same property (energy sufficient to excite electrons) underlies both uses and risks (1). Secure: 3–4 marks. Developing: 2 marks. Emerging: 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Compare the properties and uses of X-rays and infrared radiation. Include wavelength, frequency, and one use of each in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: X-rays have shorter wavelength and higher frequency than infrared (1); X-rays are ionising — used in medical imaging to show bones (1); infrared has longer wavelength and lower frequency; it is non-ionising (1); infrared is used in remote controls, thermal imaging, or optical fibre communication (1). Secure: all four points. Developing: three points. Emerging: two points.

practice_questions.text: Describe an investigation a student could carry out to compare the rate of infrared emission from surfaces with different colours and textures.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: use a Leslie cube (or beakers with differently coloured surfaces: matt black, shiny silver) filled with hot water (1); place an infrared detector at a fixed, equal distance from each surface (1); record the infrared reading for each surface under identical conditions (same water temperature, same distance) (1); compare results — matt black surface should emit most infrared (1). Secure: all four stages. Developing: three stages. Emerging: two stages.

lessons.title: Climate Models and Earth's Energy Balance

before.content_html:
The Earth’s Energy Balance

Every object emits electromagnetic radiation. The hotter the object, the greater the intensity of that radiation and the shorter its principal wavelength. The Sun is extremely hot and emits most of its energy as visible light and ultraviolet. The Earth’s surface is much cooler, so it re-emits energy mainly as infrared radiation.

For the Earth’s average temperature to remain stable, the energy arriving from the Sun must be balanced by the energy the Earth radiates back out to space. When these are in balance, the Earth is said to be in energy equilibrium. If something disrupts this balance — for example by trapping more outgoing radiation — the planet warms until a new equilibrium is reached.

Key Fact

All objects emit electromagnetic radiation. The hotter the object, the shorter the peak wavelength of the radiation it emits. The Earth is far cooler than the Sun, so it emits mainly infrared, which has a longer wavelength than visible light.

The Greenhouse Effect

The Earth’s atmosphere is not uniformly transparent. Gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour absorb outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions — including back towards the surface. This process is called the greenhouse effect. Without it, the Earth’s average surface temperature would be well below freezing, making most life impossible.

The greenhouse effect is therefore natural and essential. The concern scientists raise is the enhanced greenhouse effect: human activities since industrialisation have significantly increased the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely through burning fossil fuels and large-scale deforestation. The concentration of carbon dioxide has risen steadily over the past two centuries. This traps more infrared, shifting the Earth’s energy balance and driving global warming.

The main greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour. Carbon dioxide enters the atmosphere primarily through burning fossil fuels and deforestation. Methane is released from livestock digestion, rice paddies, landfill sites and leaks from natural gas systems. Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but its concentration is controlled mainly by temperature rather than directly by human activity.

Different greenhouse gases differ in their warming potential. Methane is a far more potent greenhouse gas per molecule than carbon dioxide, though it is present in smaller quantities. Scientists use the concept of ‘carbon dioxide equivalent’ to compare gases on a common scale.

Climate Models and the Role of Evidence

Scientists use climate models to understand past climate and to predict how it will change. These models incorporate the physics of the atmosphere, oceans and land surface, and are tested against historical temperature records, ice-core data and satellite measurements. When a model accurately reproduces past climate, scientists have greater confidence in its future projections.

This is an example of how scientific explanations develop over time (an important idea in science). Early climate models were simple; as computing power increased and more data became available, models became more detailed and their predictions more reliable. Multiple independent research groups around the world have built their own models, and the fact that different models consistently agree on the direction of warming increases confidence in the underlying science.

Key Fact

Climate models are tested using historical temperature records, ice-core data (which preserve ancient atmospheric composition) and satellite measurements of outgoing radiation. Models that reproduce past climate accurately provide more reliable projections of future change.

All scientific models have limitations. Climate models simplify enormously complex systems: they cannot perfectly represent every cloud, ocean current or feedback loop. This produces uncertainty in the exact magnitude and timing of predicted changes. Scientists communicate this uncertainty using ranges rather than single figures — for example, giving a range of possible warming values rather than one precise number.

Uncertainty does not mean ignorance. The direction of change — warming as greenhouse gas concentrations rise — is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence and is a robust conclusion. The uncertainty is mainly about how much warming will occur, not whether it will occur. This distinction is important when evaluating public and media representations of climate science.

Climate science also illustrates how the scientific community works: findings are published, subjected to peer review, replicated by other groups and refined over time. The broad agreement among climate scientists is itself a product of this rigorous process, not simply shared opinion.

Feedback Loops

One reason climate change is complex is that the climate system contains feedback loops. An example of a positive feedback: as temperatures rise, Arctic sea ice melts. Open ocean absorbs more solar radiation than white ice does, causing further warming, which melts more ice. This cycle amplifies the initial warming. Feedback loops make it harder to predict the exact pace of change and are a major source of uncertainty in climate models.
before.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about climate change and models, apply scientific reasoning rather than just recalling facts. If asked to ‘evaluate’ evidence for climate change, discuss why multiple lines of evidence (historical records, ice cores, satellite data) give scientists more confidence than any single source. If asked about model limitations, acknowledge uncertainty while explaining that uncertainty about magnitude does not undermine the overall conclusion. Distinguish between correlation and cause when discussing rising CO2 and rising temperatures — examiners want you to explain the physical mechanism (the greenhouse effect) that links them, not just note that both are rising.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Earth emits mainly infrared radiation rather than visible light.
practice_questions.marks: The Earth's surface is much cooler than the Sun [1]. Cooler objects emit radiation at longer wavelengths (lower principal frequency), so the Earth emits mainly infrared rather than visible light [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe the greenhouse effect and explain how it keeps the Earth's surface warmer than it would otherwise be.
practice_questions.marks: Greenhouse gases (e.g. carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour) absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface [1]. They re-emit this radiation in all directions, including back towards the surface [1]. This reduces the rate at which the Earth loses energy to space, keeping the surface warmer [1].

practice_questions.text: Scientists use computer climate models to make predictions about future global temperatures. Explain how scientists use evidence to increase confidence in their climate model predictions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that models are tested against historical temperature records, ice-core data and satellite measurements; notes that a model that reproduces past climate accurately is more trustworthy for future predictions; explains that multiple independent groups building models that give consistent results increases confidence; distinguishes between uncertainty in magnitude and certainty about the direction of change; mentions peer review as part of the validation process.
Secure: Identifies at least two types of evidence used to test models and links model testing to confidence in predictions.
Developing: States that scientists compare model outputs to real data, without explaining the significance.
Emerging: Vague reference to scientists using data.

practice_questions.text: A student says: 'Because climate scientists disagree about exact temperature predictions, we cannot be sure that global warming is happening.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Distinguishes clearly between uncertainty about magnitude (how much warming) and confidence about direction (that warming is occurring); explains that models contain simplifications and produce a range of predictions; argues that multiple independent lines of evidence (historical records, ice cores, satellite data, multiple model groups agreeing) all support the conclusion that warming is occurring; evaluates the student's statement as a misrepresentation of what scientific uncertainty means; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Correctly explains that uncertainty in models does not undermine the overall conclusion; references at least two lines of evidence.
Developing: Acknowledges some uncertainty but also some evidence for warming, without weighing them effectively.
Emerging: Simply agrees or disagrees with the statement without using scientific reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which human activities have increased the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks: Any two of: burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) [1]; deforestation / burning forests [1]; cement manufacture [1]. One mark each.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a positive feedback loop in the context of climate change. Use the melting of Arctic sea ice as an example.
practice_questions.marks: A positive feedback loop is one where an initial change triggers further changes that amplify the original effect [1]. As temperatures rise, Arctic sea ice melts, exposing darker ocean water [1]. The ocean absorbs more solar radiation than ice, causing additional warming, which melts more ice — amplifying the original warming [1].

before.content_html:
What Is a Wave?

A wave is a regular disturbance that transfers energy in the direction of travel without transferring matter. When ripples spread across a pond, water molecules bob up and down — they do not travel across the pond. It is the disturbance, carrying energy, that moves outwards.

Waves are described by four key quantities. The amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position — a larger amplitude means a more energetic wave. The wavelength (symbol λ) is the distance between two successive identical points — for example, from crest to crest. The frequency (symbol f) is the number of complete waves passing a fixed point per second, measured in hertz (Hz). The period is the time for one complete wave to pass, measured in seconds.

Key Fact

Wave speed, frequency and wavelength are related by the wave equation:
$$v = f \times \lambda$$ where \(v\) is wave speed in m/s, \(f\) is frequency in Hz and \(\lambda\) is wavelength in m. This applies to all waves — water ripples, sound and all electromagnetic waves.

Transverse and Longitudinal Waves

Waves fall into two types depending on the direction of the disturbance relative to the direction of energy transfer. In a transverse wave, the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel. Waves on a rope are a clear example: flick one end and the displacement is up-and-down while the energy travels along the rope. All electromagnetic waves are transverse.

In a longitudinal wave, the oscillations are parallel to the direction of travel. Sound waves in air are longitudinal: the air pressure alternately increases (compressions) and decreases (rarefactions) along the direction the sound moves. A slinky spring being pushed and pulled along its length is a useful physical model.

Question: A sound wave in air has a frequency of 440 Hz and a wavelength of 0.77 m. Calculate its wave speed.

Step 1 — identify the equation: \(v = f \times \lambda\)

Step 2 — substitute values: \(v = 440 \text{ Hz} \times 0.77 \text{ m}\)

Step 3 — calculate: \(v = 338.8 \text{ m/s}\)

This is close to the accepted speed of sound in air at room temperature (approximately 340 m/s), confirming the calculation is reasonable. Always check your answer makes physical sense.

Reflection

When a wave meets a boundary between two materials, it may be reflected, refracted or transmitted (or some combination). Reflection occurs when a wave bounces off a surface. The angle of incidence (measured from the normal — a line perpendicular to the surface) equals the angle of reflection. A smooth surface reflects waves in one direction (specular reflection), while a rough surface scatters them in many directions.

Refraction

Refraction happens when a wave passes from one medium into another and changes speed. Waves travel at different speeds in different substances, and these speeds may also vary with wavelength — which is why a prism splits white light into colours. Because the frequency of a wave cannot change (it is set by the source), a change in speed produces a change in wavelength. If the wave also hits the boundary at an angle, it changes direction. Light entering glass slows down, causing it to bend towards the normal. Light leaving glass speeds up and bends away from the normal.

Key Fact

Refraction is caused by a change in wave speed at a boundary. Frequency stays constant, so wavelength changes. If the wave hits the boundary at an angle, the direction of travel changes too. Waves slow down when entering a denser medium and speed up when leaving it. Wave speed can vary with wavelength, which is why different colours refract by different amounts.

A ripple tank can be used to measure the speed, frequency and wavelength of water waves. A vibrating dipper creates waves of known frequency. The wavelength is measured from photographs or stroboscopic images of the wave pattern, and wave speed is calculated using \(v = f \times \lambda\). The tank also allows students to observe reflection (using barriers) and refraction (using a shallow section, which slows the wave).

The speed of sound in air can be measured by timing an echo over a known distance. A clap near a wall, with an observer recording the time for the echo to return, gives a simple measure. More precisely, two microphones separated by a measured distance can be used with a data logger to time how long the sound takes to travel between them.

The Wave Model and Its Limits

The wave model is a powerful tool: it successfully predicts the behaviour of light and sound at boundaries, explains colour and musical pitch, and underpins technologies from radio to medical imaging. However, like all scientific models, it has limitations. At very small scales (atomic and subatomic), light also behaves as a stream of particles called photons — a description captured in quantum physics. The fact that wave and particle descriptions are both needed to fully explain light’s behaviour is an example of how scientific models develop as new evidence emerges. For your GCSE, the wave model is sufficient for all the topics assessed.

Understanding waves also connects to the electromagnetic spectrum — all electromagnetic waves are transverse and travel at the same speed through a vacuum. Their different properties (radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma) depend on their frequency and wavelength. The wave equation \(v = f \times \lambda\) applies to every one of them.
before.exam_tip_html: Questions on the wave equation \(v = f \times \lambda\) are straightforward if you identify which two quantities are given and rearrange correctly — practise rearranging for \(f\) and \(\lambda\) as well as \(v\). When explaining refraction, always state that it is caused by a change in speed, and that frequency remains constant — just saying “the wave bends” will not earn full marks. For questions about transverse vs longitudinal waves, a common error is saying sound is transverse; remember that sound in air is always longitudinal. Extended response questions on wave behaviour reward clear use of scientific language: use terms such as normal, angle of incidence, wavelength and medium rather than vague phrases like “it slows down and changes direction”.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. They are described by amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period; the wave equation \(v = f \times \lambda\) links speed, frequency and wavelength.
  • Transverse waves (e.g. light, water ripples) oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel; longitudinal waves (e.g. sound) oscillate parallel to the direction of travel.
  • Reflection bounces a wave off a surface (angle of incidence = angle of reflection); refraction occurs when a wave changes speed at a boundary, causing a change in wavelength and, if the wave strikes at an angle, a change in direction.

practice_questions.text: A water wave has a frequency of 3 Hz and a wavelength of 0.2 m. Calculate the wave speed.
practice_questions.marks: \(v = f \times \lambda = 3 \times 0.2\) [1] = 0.6 m/s [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Transverse: oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer [1]; example such as light / water waves / waves on a rope [1]. Longitudinal: oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer [1]; example such as sound / compression of a slinky [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why a beam of light changes direction when it passes from air into glass.
practice_questions.marks: Light slows down when it enters glass [1]. The frequency stays constant, so the wavelength decreases [1]. When the wave hits the boundary at an angle, the change in speed causes the direction of travel to change (towards the normal) [1].

practice_questions.text: A student uses a ripple tank to measure wave speed. Describe how the student could measure the wavelength and frequency of the waves in the tank.
practice_questions.marks: Frequency: count the number of complete waves passing a fixed point per second (or use a stroboscope to freeze the pattern at a known frequency) [1]; record multiple counts and take an average to improve reliability [1]. Wavelength: take a photograph or stroboscopic image of the wave pattern; measure the distance across several wavelengths and divide by the number [1]; identify crest-to-crest distance as one wavelength [1].

practice_questions.text: A radio wave has a speed of \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s and a wavelength of 1500 m. Calculate its frequency.
practice_questions.marks: Rearrange \(v = f \times \lambda\) to give \(f = v \div \lambda\) [1]. \(f = (3 \times 10^8) \div 1500 = 2 \times 10^5\) Hz (200 000 Hz) [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain what happens to the wavelength and speed of a light wave as it passes from glass back into air.
practice_questions.marks: As the wave crosses the boundary into air its speed increases [1]. Frequency does not change [1]. Since \(v = f \times \lambda\), an increase in speed at constant frequency means the wavelength increases [1].

before.content_html:
Specular Reflection and Diffuse Scattering

When a beam of light hits a smooth, polished surface such as a mirror, all the rays reflect at the same angle — the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal. This is called specular reflection. Because all rays reflect uniformly, a clear image is formed.

Most everyday surfaces are not perfectly smooth. An uneven surface scatters incoming light in many different directions — this is diffuse reflection. This is why you can see a piece of paper from any angle but cannot see your reflection in it.

Refraction, Prisms and Dispersion

Light is refracted when it changes speed at a boundary. When white light passes through a glass prism, the different colours within it travel at slightly different speeds in glass, so they refract by slightly different amounts. Violet light (shortest visible wavelength) is refracted the most; red light (longest visible wavelength) is refracted the least. The beam spreads into the colours of the spectrum. This spreading is called dispersion.

Key Fact

White light is a mixture of all visible colours, ranging from violet (shortest wavelength) to red (longest wavelength). A prism disperses white light into a spectrum because different wavelengths travel at different speeds in glass, causing different amounts of refraction. Violet refracts the most; red refracts the least.

Colour, Absorption and Transmission

A coloured filter works by transmitting light of some wavelengths and absorbing light of others. A red filter transmits red wavelengths and absorbs all others, which is why only red light passes through it.

An object’s apparent colour depends on which wavelengths it scatters (reflects diffusely). An object appears white if it scatters all colours equally; it appears black if it absorbs all colours and scatters none. A red tomato scatters red wavelengths and absorbs the rest. This means the colour you perceive depends on the light falling on the object: a red object under only blue light will appear dark (because there is no red light to scatter).

A convex lens (converging lens) is thicker at the centre. It refracts parallel rays inwards so they meet at a focal point on the far side. Convex lenses are used in cameras, eyes and magnifying glasses. A concave lens (diverging lens) is thinner at the centre. It refracts parallel rays outwards so they appear to spread from a point on the same side as the incoming light. Concave lenses are used in glasses to correct short-sightedness.

A real image is formed when refracted rays actually converge at a point; it can be projected onto a screen. A virtual image appears to come from a point but the rays do not actually meet there; it cannot be projected.

Sound Transmission Through Solids

Sound travels as a longitudinal wave, and it travels better through solids and liquids than through air — because the particles are closer together and transmit vibrations more efficiently. This is why you can hear sound through a wall more easily when you press your ear against it.

The bones in the middle ear are a biological example of sound transmission through a solid. The three small bones (malleus, incus and stapes) transmit vibrations from the eardrum to the fluid of the inner ear. These bones transmit sound most efficiently in the frequency range from about 1 kHz to about 3 kHz — which corresponds well with the frequencies most important for understanding speech. This limited frequency response is the reason human hearing has the range it does.

Key Fact

Sound travels faster and more efficiently through solids and liquids than through gases, because particles are closer together and transmit vibrations more readily. The bones in the middle ear transmit sound vibrations most efficiently in the 1 kHz to 3 kHz range, which is the frequency range of normal speech.

The ways in which sound waves are transmitted, reflected and refracted as they pass through different materials are exploited in several technologies. In medical ultrasound imaging, high-frequency sound waves above the range of human hearing are directed into the body. Reflections from boundaries between different tissue types return to a detector and are used to build up an image.

SONAR (Sound Navigation And Ranging) works on a similar principle in water: pulses of sound are sent out from a vessel and the time for reflections to return is used to calculate the depth of the sea floor or the position of objects such as fish shoals. Earthquake (seismic) waves, which travel through the Earth, have revealed details of the Earth’s layered internal structure because different types of seismic wave are reflected and refracted differently at boundaries between rock layers. The differences in velocity, absorption and reflection between wave types allow scientists to map structures hidden from direct observation.

Transmission, Absorption and Scattering

When a wave meets a material, three things can happen: it may be transmitted (pass through), absorbed (its energy transferred to the material) or reflected and scattered. Most real encounters involve a combination of all three, in proportions that depend on the wavelength of the wave and the nature of the material. A clear glass window transmits visible light but absorbs some infrared; a coloured glass transmits selected wavelengths and absorbs others; an opaque wall absorbs all visible light and transmits none.

The principle extends to sound. Soft furnishings in a concert hall absorb sound, reducing echo and reverberation. Hard surfaces reflect sound, which can cause unwanted echoes. Acoustic engineers designing concert halls and recording studios use knowledge of sound transmission, absorption and reflection to control how sound behaves in a space. The same considerations apply to building construction: thick, dense walls transmit less sound than thin partitions because more of the wave energy is absorbed within the material.
before.conclusion_html:
• Specular reflection from smooth surfaces produces clear images; diffuse reflection from rough surfaces scatters light in all directions. A prism disperses white light into a spectrum because different wavelengths refract by different amounts — violet most, red least.
  • Coloured filters transmit some wavelengths and absorb others; an object’s apparent colour is determined by which wavelengths it scatters. Convex lenses converge light to a real image; concave lenses diverge it to produce a virtual image.
  • Sound travels better through solids and liquids than through air; the ear bones transmit vibrations most efficiently in the 1–3 kHz range. Ultrasound imaging, SONAR and earthquake seismology all exploit reflection and refraction of sound in materials.
before.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about colour and filters, make sure you use the words ‘transmit’ and ‘absorb’ precisely rather than just ‘let through’ or ‘block’. For questions about lenses, remember that a convex lens converges rays (they meet on the far side) and produces a real image that can be projected, while a concave lens diverges rays and produces a virtual image. In questions on sound transmission, be specific: explain that sound travels faster in solids because particles are closer together, not just ‘because it’s denser’. For questions on the ear, state the frequency range (approximately 1–3 kHz) explicitly if the mark scheme looks numerical.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between specular reflection and diffuse reflection. Give one example of a surface that produces each type.
practice_questions.marks: Specular reflection: occurs at smooth surfaces; all parallel incident rays reflect at the same angle; produces a clear image [1]; example such as a mirror or still water surface [1]. Diffuse reflection: occurs at rough or uneven surfaces; rays are scattered in many directions; no clear image formed [1]; example such as paper, a wall or wood [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why a red filter appears red when white light shines through it.
practice_questions.marks: The filter absorbs light of all wavelengths except red [1]. Red wavelengths are transmitted through the filter, so the filter appears red [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe how a convex lens forms a real image of a distant object. Use the terms focal point and converge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Parallel rays of light from the distant object enter the convex lens [1]. The lens refracts the rays, causing them to converge [1]. The rays meet at the focal point on the far side of the lens, forming a real image that can be projected onto a screen [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why sound travels faster through bone than through air.
practice_questions.marks: Sound travels as a longitudinal wave, involving vibrations of particles [1]. In bone, the particles are much closer together than in air [1]. Closer particles transfer vibrations more quickly (less energy is lost between particles), so the wave travels faster [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain how SONAR is used to measure the depth of water beneath a ship.
practice_questions.marks: A pulse of sound (ultrasound) is sent downwards from the ship [1]. The pulse is reflected from the sea floor and returns to a detector on the ship [1]. The time between sending the pulse and receiving the echo is measured; using the known speed of sound in water, the depth can be calculated using: depth = (speed × time) ÷ 2 [1].

practice_questions.text: A student shines a beam of white light through a glass prism and sees a spectrum. Explain why violet light is refracted more than red light.
practice_questions.marks: White light is a mixture of colours with different wavelengths [1]. Different wavelengths travel at slightly different speeds in glass [1]. Violet light travels more slowly in glass than red light (so it refracts more at the boundary), causing a larger change in direction [1].

options: Diffuse reflection from a rough surface
Specular reflection from a smooth surface
Total internal reflection from a lens
Absorption of all wavelengths by the surface

knowledge_checks.q: What does a convex (converging) lens do to parallel rays of light?
options: Spreads them outward, creating a virtual image
Reflects them back towards the source
Brings them together at a focal point, creating a real image
Absorbs most wavelengths, transmitting only red light

The bones in the middle ear transmit sound vibrations most efficiently in the frequency range from about _____ to 3 kHz.
Match each optical term to its correct description.
right: Scattering of light in many directions from a rough surface
Separation of white light into its component colours by a prism
Transmits certain wavelengths and absorbs others
